title: Every Day Waakye
author: Fran Osseo-Asare
desc: From dried beans — boiled briefly, soaked an hour, then cooked covered with the rice until both are done, watching that it does not burn.
longDesc: The version made from dried beans rather than a tin, and the one most like how waakye is actually cooked in Ghana. A cup of dried black-eyed peas is boiled briefly, soaked an hour and drained, then cooked with a teaspoon of baking soda, a cup of rice, half a cup of chopped onion, a tablespoon of oil, a teaspoon of salt and two and a half cups of water, covered, until the rice and beans are cooked. Her warning is the whole difficulty of the dish: watch out that it does not burn. A full teaspoon of soda here, against half to one in the tinned version.
steps: Boil the dried black-eyed peas briefly.
Put the drained peas, baking soda, rice, onion, oil, salt and water into the pot.
Cover and cook until the rice and beans are cooked.
Watch out that it does not burn.
chefTips: Watch out that it does not burn — her own warning and the reason the rice-cooker version exists. The beans release starch and the base catches easily.
The quick-boil-and-hour-soak is a shortcut for an overnight soak. It works and it saves the planning.
A full teaspoon of baking soda here, against half to one in the tinned version. Dried beans need more alkali to soften and colour.
Two and a half cups of water for a cup of rice plus a cup of dried beans. The beans are only partly hydrated after an hour, so they drink a good deal.
Drain after soaking. The soaking water carries the compounds that cause wind, and discarding it is standard practice.
Dried beans give a far better texture than tinned — they hold their shape and taste of something. This is the version worth the extra time.
No doneness cue beyond until the rice and beans are cooked, so taste a bean rather than trusting a clock.
commonMistakes: Leaving it unwatched, so the base burns.
Using the tinned version's lower soda amount.
Judging doneness by the rice alone rather than the beans.
sources: Adapted from version 2, 'Every Day Waakye', within 'Recipe #27: Waakye 3 ways (rice and beans)', betumiblog.blogspot.com, 9 November 2009. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Posted by Fran at 11:03 PM'. NO YIELD LINE is printed. Quantities confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS).
Ingredients exactly as printed: 1 cup black-eyed peas; 1 teaspoon baking soda; 1 cup rice; 1/2 cup chopped onion; 1 tablespoon oil; 1 teaspoon salt; 2 1/2 cups water.
Method as printed, SINGLE-PASS: boil briefly, soak an hour, drain; cook covered 'until the rice and beans are cooked. Watch out that it doesn't burn.'
THE WARNING is the only cue the version gives and it is reproduced as the step it is rather than demoted to a tip.

THE THIRD VERSION ON THE SAME PAGE, recorded here rather than published as its own entry because it is a coconut variant rather than a distinct method: 'Special' waakye, confirmed on both fetches — 1 cup black-eyed peas; 1 teaspoon baking soda; 1 cup rice; 1 teaspoon salt; 1/2 cup onion; 1 cup water or coconut milk; 2 tablespoons coconut cream; thyme or oregano. The '3 cups of water (initial)' figure is SINGLE-PASS. Its method, SINGLE-PASS: simmer the beans with the soda 30 minutes, then 'cook, covered, until the rice and beans are tender, about half an hour'. NOTE that thyme or oregano in waakye appears in no other documented version.

THE WATER DISAGREEMENT ACROSS THE THREE VERSIONS, all by one author on one page, recorded and NOT averaged: 2 cups (tinned peas, GHA058), 2½ cups (dried peas, here), and 1 cup water or coconut milk plus a SINGLE-PASS '3 cups of water (initial)' in the Special version. The baking soda also differs: ½ to 1 teaspoon in the tinned version against a full teaspoon in both dried-bean versions.
For the colouring-agent note, the waakye tray and the named gap on jollof-versus-waakye, see the sources at GHA058.
reheating: Steam, or microwave with a splash of water.
healthBenefits: Dried beans retain more fibre and resistant starch than tinned.
Rice and black-eyed peas together give a complete protein.
High in folate, iron and soluble fibre.
Discarding the soaking water reduces the oligosaccharides that cause wind.
culturalNote: Every day waakye is the honest name for it — this is the pot that gets made at home rather than the shortcut, and the burning warning is what every Ghanaian cook knows without being told. The alkaline soda doing the work that millet leaves do in a village pot is the one genuine substitution in the recipe.
